segments.text: Welcome to Many Minds, a podcast about our world's spectacular varieties of mind
and what we can learn from them. We feature conversations that shed light on the diverse
ways of thinking, sensing, and being that are out there. I'm your host, Kenzie Cooperrider.
Thanks for joining us. Preferences, decisions, goals. When you hear these words, you probably
think of humans. Or, if not humans, then maybe charismatic animals. You know, great apes,
certain species of birds, maybe dogs. In any case, I bet you think of creatures that are more
or less cognitively sophisticated. I know I do. But, according to some researchers, this is an
outmoded and over-narrow way of thinking. They propose that decisions and goals, not to mention
other fancy-seeming constructs like memory, problem-solving, and intelligence, can usefully
be ascribed to an astonishingly large array of agents. Not just humans, not just animals,
not even just organisms. My guest on today's episode is Dr. Michael Levin. He's the Vannevar
Bush Distinguished Professor of Biology at Tufts University. He directs the Allen Discovery Center
and the Tufts Center for Regenerative and Developmental Biology. In recent years, Mike's
been developing a radical reconsideration of the nature of mind and intelligence. He argues that
it's not just humans and other smart creatures that traffic in all this classically cognitive
stuff. It's also cells, tissues, organs, colonial organisms, and much more. He sometimes summarizes
his view as cognition all the way down. Here, we talk about how Mike came to this perspective.
We discuss his empirical studies of bioelectricity, including some pretty astonishing experiments
on planaria. We dig deep into two of the conceptual models Mike uses in talking about this mind
everywhere framework, the axis of persuadability, and the notion of the cognitive light cone.
And we talk about why Mike rejects the criticism that this is all just mere anthropomorphism.
In fact, he makes a compelling case that it's time we retired that term altogether.
You know, in the intro to many minds, way back when, we talked about how the train of mind is vast.
But as I've learned about the work of Mike and others, I've become increasingly convinced that
the train of mind is actually vaster than I ever imagined at the time. Maybe vastly vaster.
I think you'll like this one, folks. And even if you're not convinced, there's little doubt you'll
be provoked. So without further preamble, onto my conversation with Dr. Michael Levin. Enjoy.
Mike Levin, welcome to Many Minds.
Thank you. Yeah, really happy to be here. Thanks.
So one thing that people may not have guessed about you just from the fact that you're a biologist is
that you also seem to be quite a book person. I say this both because behind you, as we're doing
this interview, you've got an impressive wall of books. And also on your Twitter feed, you do a lot
of shout outs to books, often older books. So can you tell us a little bit about your book,
your relationship to books?
Yeah. Well, I love to read from an early age. My dad and I spent pretty much every weekend in
used bookstores. That was a, you know, when I was younger, that was a thing we used to do every
Saturday. We'd go down to Cambridge or other places and just hit the old bookstores. And I'd come back
with a pile and you can, you know, you can sort of see them all here. Yeah. And so I'm just, you know,
on Twitter, I'm just going left to right one per day and just, yeah, just pulling out some of the
ones that I think people will enjoy.
Yeah, definitely. And people do enjoy them. All right. So eventually where I thought we
could go in this conversation is to talk about all kinds of big stuff, preferences, selves,
agency, memory, decisions, intelligence, all that stuff. But I thought we, you know,
we could maybe start a little more concretely. So in recent papers and some talks that I've seen you
give, you've mentioned this example of what happens to caterpillars on their way to becoming
butterflies. So could you say a little bit about that?
Sure. Yeah. I mean, one of the ways that people talk about issues about around philosophy of mind
and cognition and so on is to pick a subject. So they have an animal and it might be a rat or
an octopus or something. And then they talk about what that creature does and its memories and various
things. And so I think one of the things that really sheds light on a lot of these problems is
to keep in mind that the subject of cognition, so the owner of memories, the owner of preferences and
all of that is really not fixed and can change. And one of the, over time, both evolutionary time,
but also over the time of the lifetime of the agent. So the caterpillars, lots of people study
behavior in caterpillars, lots of people study behavior in butterflies. But what happens when a
caterpillar becomes a butterfly is that their brain is largely recreated. So many of the neurons die,
most of the connections are broken. An entirely new brain is created that is appropriate now,
instead of being a soft-bodied creature that chews plants, now you're a flying, hard-bodied creature
that has to drink nectar. So the brain is completely different. And by the way, memories persist during
this process. So things that a caterpillar learns, the butterfly or the moth also remembers. So that raises
really interesting questions about what it's like to be an agent when the substrate of your cognition,
the brain or whatever, whatever else is, is, is important for your cognitive capacities is
literally changing in real time during the lifetime of the agent, which is completely different from
saying though, you know, over evolutionary, the histories, brains change and so on. This is one
creature, one agent drastically changing during its lifetime. And of course we all do during embryonic
development. We start life as a bunch of cells and then eventually we become, you know, this is this
hopefully advanced cognitive for being. So yeah, I think, I think that kind of example is really
helpful to make sure that our, our various concepts in our theories hold water in the sense that they're
not just applying to some fixed, unchanging, you know, agent that, that is supposed to be this
indivisible thing that just is the way it is. Right. Right. And I guess this, this also connects
to ideas about how, you know, in an adult human, there's turnover of cells, there's turnover of neurons
and that sort of thing. So even though we may have the illusion that we ourselves are those sort of
fixed, unchanging agents, that's actually not necessarily true at the cellular level. Is that
right? Most certainly. And not only were we an agent that changed drastically when our whole brain and
everything else was put together by the activity of cells during development. And of course, during
adulthood, all of our cells are turning over and so on, but actually even, even biomedically,
this is going to be a very important point that within the next, you know, I don't know exactly,
but probably in the next decade or two, we are going to have treatments for let's say degenerative
diseases of the brain, where adult human patients are going to be injected with stem cells, which are
hopefully going to repopulate the brain. So the progeny of these exogenous stem cells are going to
be re replacing parts of the brains of a living patient with five, six decades of memories of
personality and so on. So what happens during that time when there's this, this like radical change of
the, of the architecture of the brain? I mean, no, no one knows, right? So people can do work in
models like axolotl, like planaria that let you do behavior and regeneration in the same animal,
but yeah, we're, we're heading for a time where that will become an actual, an actual question that
biomedicine is going to have to face. All right. Well, that's a good little teaser of some of the
terrain we're going to go into, but I thought we could actually step back a little bit and talk about
some of your earlier work that kind of got you headed in these directions. So one of your
longstanding interest has been in bioelectricity and bioelectricity as a major force in morphogenesis
in the emergence of a biological form. So could you tell us a little bit about, I guess, how you
got into bioelectricity and some of the stuff you've learned about it? Yeah. So, so I've been
interested in bioelectricity since I was probably 16 or 17 years old. And the reason is, and it's,
and it's not obvious tracing the, the publications, you know, through my, through my career is that,
I originally got into it because it seemed to me really interesting that the mechanisms that
evolution used to orchestrate the decisions of morphogenesis, right? So the collection of cells
that have to get together and as a collective agent, they have to decide what they're going
to build. And then they build various organs and various body, body structures and so on that,
that, that process. And, and the fact that that process might be orchestrated by electrical
signaling, which people have been making that claim for well over a hundred years.
And so I came across when I was, when I was 17, um, I was at a, uh, at the world's fair
in Vancouver and I was at a used bookstore with my dad and I found a Becker's book,
the body electric and Becker in that book talks about many things, but among them cite some really
old and more or less at the time forgotten literature on how electrical signaling among cells
that are not neurons help determine the shape of the body. So the structures of the, of the structure
of the body. And it hit me that this is, this is incredibly interesting because brains of course,
use that same system to make decisions during behavior and to process information and store
memories and so on. And of course, in computer science, we use that same type of modality to do
computations and to try to implement artificial intelligence and so on. And so the fact that,
that there was this, this remarkable, um, invariance, right. That this thing was all across from the
creation and the solving of problems about body structure to behavior, to intelligence and memory
and so on that struck me as very interesting. And so while my early work was always, uh, framed as
investigating bioelectricity as a developmental modality for patterning, you know, as we have,
we have chemical gradients and we have biomechanics and now look, we have bioelectricity,
right. So cells communicate electrically and that determines organ structure and size and all that,
you know, for years, that was the way I sort of presented this. And what I think is really
interesting about bioelectricity is not simply that yes, it is a modality by which cells work together
and make and implement particular things, but it's also the computational layer by, by tracking the
bioelectricity, you get direct access to the cognitive layer of that swarm intelligence of cells.
And it's exactly the same as what people who work on neural decoding and neuroscience do,
right. They, they think that by, by tracking the electrical activity in the brain, they will be
able to decode that and say something about the, the plans, the thoughts, the preferences,
the memories of the creature. And I think that's exactly also true for, for basal cognition in
morphogenesis. And so only recently, you know, I've, I've, I've started only recently emphasizing that
in the work because frankly, because we had to establish a set of a set of methods, a set of
data to kind of put this, this field on a firm footing first, before we could start linking it
to the basal cognition field. It would just be, you know, I don't think anybody would have paid
attention if I said on day one, that, that I thought it was all about basal cognition and
morphogenesis, but now both fields are ripe that we can actually make that connection.
All right. Well, so we'll come back to this, this term you're using basal cognition and talk a
little bit about what's kind of going on in that field, but just to linger a little bit on the
bioelectricity. So in case listeners aren't aware, how would you describe the contribution of
bioelectricity over and above genetic information in kind of generating biological form? How do you
think about kind of the collaboration there? Yeah. So, so let's, maybe we take one step back and
just say what bioelectricity is, because I want to be clear that this is not about electromagnetic
fields. It's not about waves or applied electricity with electrodes or anything like that. So the best
way to think about this is if we start with the brain and work backwards. So in the brain, you have
a system where you have a network of cells. These neurons are all connected to each other. Every
neuron is able to drive a particular, what we call a resting potential. So this is just a voltage around
the, across the membrane. And it might be, you know, minus 80 millivolts or something like that.
And all of these neurons are connected with each other and they're able to propagate their electrical
state to other cells. And there are some complicated rules about how these signals are propagated. And
as a result, you have this complicated network that's able to do some computations and it has
some memory and it has many, many, many other things. So one can ask, where did this all come
from? Did neurons just sort of suddenly appear out of nowhere? When did evolution develop this trick
of being able to compute via electricity? And it turns out that if you track the development of
nervous systems backwards, you find out that the things that neurons are doing existed all the
way back in unicellular ancestors. So in fact, around the time of bacterial biofilms, and there's
some beautiful new work on this, even around the time of bacterial biofilms, evolution had already
figured out that networks of electrical activity are a very convenient and powerful way to process
information. All cells have ion channels like neurons have. Most cells have these electrical
synapses with each other where they're called gap junctions and they allow the electrical states
to propagate. So this goes all the way back. And so all the way during, at the first steps of
embryogenesis, when the egg divides, and now there are multiple early cells sitting there,
that whole collective, those cells need to make a lot of anatomical decisions because somebody is,
some of them have to become anterior, some have to become posterior, dorsal, ventral,
left and right, and then they have to make the various organs, lots of things to be figured out.
And so I think that what bioelectricity does is it serves as an important part of the software
that allows the genetically specified hardware to do its job. And now, to be clear, bioelectricity is
not the only thing that does it. There are also, of course, chemical gradients, there are biomechanics,
and so on. But I think bioelectricity is particularly interesting because it's particularly
important for this specific side of things where I think what the genome does is it specifies the
hardware. The genome tells every cell what ion channels and other proteins it gets to have.
And so let's be clear, when you read the genome, you don't see directly any information about the
animal structure or the plant structure. So you're not going to see directly, okay, it's got bilateral
symmetry, it's got four legs, two eyes, you don't see any of that in the genome. All you see in the
genome is a specification of the micro level hardware of each cell, what proteins every cell
is going to have. Once the genome, once that machine is built, so the cells are there, they're
expressing the genes, you have a bunch of cells. It's the equivalent of turning on an electric circuit,
it has some default behavior. According to the laws of physics, the electricity will propagate in
various ways, that system will generate some default outputs, which break symmetry and make,
you know, they make one part of the animal different from the other part and various other
things. Working together with chemistry and biomechanics, the bioelectricity is a huge part
of the software of life. It's what allows that collection of cells to work together as a collective
intelligence that is going to build whatever it is that it's going to build.
So I gather that your work on bioelectricity has recently led you to do some pretty cool and
mind-blowing experiments with planaria, where you actually sort of manipulate the form of
planaria by manipulating the bioelectricity in the organism. Can you tell us a little bit about
some of that work? Sure. So planaria are these flatworms that they're an amazing model system
because they're fairly advanced. They have a centralized brain, they have a nervous system,
lots of different organ types and cell types and so on. And the amazing thing about planaria is that
when they are injured, or if you were to cut them into pieces and the record, I think it's something
like 275 pieces, you cut them into pieces, every piece will regrow exactly what's needed, no more,
no less to make a perfect tiny little worm. So now this is very interesting because it highlights
the fact of, and this is called regeneration and the fact of regeneration highlights a really critical
part of this whole process. Because if you, if you just think about embryonic development,
one way to think about it is, okay, there are local rules, sort of like a cellular automaton
that people model in mathematics, where there are local rules, every cell follows these little
rules. And then eventually, you know, millions and millions of cells do this. And then eventually
something complex comes out and that's the end of it. And so that way of thinking about it sees
morphogenesis as a purely feed forward kind of thing, right? It just progresses forward. It's the
paradigm of emergence, complex things happening in parallel, and then voila, there's your body.
And that's that. Planaria, and in fact, regeneration in general, are telling us something much more
interesting because you can take an adult planarian and you can cut it into pieces.
And the fact that, that they regenerate is amazing, but even more amazing is that they stop.
How do they know when to stop? So one of the things that they do is they continue to,
they continue to grow and the cells proliferate and they migrate and all these things happen.
They remodel the rest of the worm gets smaller so that the growth doesn't look out of proportion
with, you know, what's there. It's amazing. All of that happens. And then they stop. And when do
they stop, they stop when they have created a correct planarian shape, and then they stop.
So what you see there is not just a feed forward system, but you see a cycle. And that cycle is
basically what we call anatomical homeostasis. Think about your thermostat, right? Your thermostat
is able to keep the temperature because if you deviate the temperature in the room off of what the
correct temperature is supposed to be, it will undergo various activities, heating, cooling, whatever,
to get you back to where you're supposed to be. Okay. So this is called homeostasis. Now homeostasis
has a couple of important pieces to this. In order to do this, you have to A, be able to measure
right now, what is my shape? Okay. Number two, you have to be able to remember what the correct
shape is. And you have to say, okay, is my shape right now correct or not? Number three, if the answer
is no, my shape is not correct. You have to undergo various activities to try to reduce that delta,
that error, right? And then you go through the loop again and you say, how about now? How about now?
And so you keep doing this in parallel and eventually that error becomes acceptably small
and then the whole thing stops. So this is one way of looking at this. It's not the only way,
but it's one way of looking at the system as a pattern, a homeostatic system. And there are two
kind of unique things about this. One is that of course, biologists all know about feedback loops
and everyone knows, knows feedback loops, but what's unique about this is two things. Number one
is that it suggests that the set point of this process, right? The key to all these homeostatic
processes is having a set point. You have to know what the correct shape is or the correct range.
Normally biologists think about homeostasis in one variable, it's temperature or it's pH or it's
hunger level, or it's, you know, it's one, one thing. This has a much more complex homeostatic
set point, which is the shape of a planarian. That's a, that's a geometric piece of information.
And so that's a kind of memory, right? That's a kind of pattern memory where you literally have to
store roughly not down to the individual cell level, but you have to store what does a correct
planarian look like so that, you know, when you see it so that you can stop, you can stop back.
So, right. So that's the first thing. The second thing is that it's, it's an interesting kind of
goal directed process. And I'm sure we'll talk more about this today, but it's one of the first
times you see in biology where it's not just, here's a bunch of chemistry that happens, but it's
actually a process that is aiming at spending energy to reach a particular goal. And when it's deviated
from that goal with injury or with anything else, it does its darndest to get back to where it is.
It's a goal directed process. So, so already you're seeing something kind of unusual. And then that
brings up a really important question, which is that if you're going to have this process,
which has some kind of encoded set point or a pattern memory, where is it? What's the pattern
memory? And so, and so this is an idea, nobody in biology is going to buy this thing because people
really don't like goals and goal directed processes. We can talk about why that is, but no one's going to buy
this unless you actually find where the pattern memory is. And the interesting thing about finding
it is, is one of two things. First of all, that it means that if you can find it, perhaps you can
rewrite it. And if you can rewrite it, the cool thing about these homeostatic systems is that you
can just change the set point and you don't have to rewire the machine. You don't have to change the
hardware. So when you have a thermostat and you now want to cool, you want to set your room to a
different temperature, you don't go rewiring the whole thermostat. You don't have to,
you just change the set point and the machine does what it always does, which is just act to the new
set point. So that means that could we find in the planarian an actual set point, we call it a
target morphology representation in tissue that guides the idea of what a correct planarian is
supposed to look like. So we did this experiment and it of course was related to other things we
had done in bioelectricity, but also you can simply ask this question. We know other goal directed
systems, brains, right? You have goals and mouse will run through the maze and get the reward and
all that. How are those goals encoded? Well, we know, we know a little bit about it, partly
bioelectrically. So we said, okay, could there be a bioelectric map, a pre-pattern in the planarian
tissues distributed that tell this animal how many heads it's supposed to have? We just boiled it all
down to a very simple question, how many heads, right? And then later on we address like with the
shape of the head and so on. So how many heads? And so what we found, but by using, we developed this
technique using voltage sensitive fluorescent dyes. So these are just molecules that you soak
your sample and the fluorescence that you catch with a microscope tells you where all the voltage
gradients are and what they are. So you look on the planarian and you see an amazing thing. You see
that there's actually a voltage gradient head to tail that is indicative of the anatomical layout of
the body. And so that of course is just observation that doesn't prove that it's doing anything. So the
next experiment is actually change the voltage. Now, how do we change the voltage? We don't use
electrodes or anything like that. We control the ion channels, the proteins that create that voltage
gradient in the first place. And so by manipulating those ion channels and by manipulating the gap
junctions, the ability of the cells to pass electrical information to each other, we were able to create
two-headed worms. So now what we in effect do is alter that electrical pattern so that the back end of
the worm, which normally has a pattern that's associated with making a tail now has a pattern
that's associated with the head and the cells, the cells simply build to that pattern and they make a
two-headed worm. Now that that's already pretty cool because, because that means that the bioelectrics is
actually instructive in determining the head shape. But what's really amazing is that I've been calling
this a pattern memory. So the amazing thing is that one of the students in my lab then decided to recut
these two-headed worms in plain water, no more manipulations of any kind, just recut them in
plain old water. And of course, think about the traditional prediction of that, right? So basically
what you do is you cut off both heads, you leave the middle fragment. So now, right? So the primary
head is gone, that ectopic secondary head is gone. People will say, well, maybe you've epigenetically
reprogrammed those cells to be a head and that's fine, but they're gone. You throw them out and throw them
away. And so now you have this middle gut fragment and the genetics are untouched. We haven't done
any genomic editing. We haven't done transgenes. We haven't knocked anything out or knocked anything
down. So you would think that then the tissue would have to build a perfectly normal one-headed
planarian, right? Because the ectopic heads are gone. The tissue has not been, the genome has not been
edited. In fact, those animals also continue to make two-headed worms as far as we can tell forever. And so what
that means is that the electrical circuit keeps a one of two states, one-headed or two-headed,
and we can, in fact, we can also make no-headed worms. It keeps that, that electrical information
and that electrical information is independent from the genome. The same exact genome is perfectly
compatible with a scenario where it will continually churn out two-headed animals. And so that's right.
And so, so that sounds pretty, pretty weird when you think of, you know, the, the genome as,
as determining, you know, everything, but we already have a class of, in fact, we have two classes of
devices that have this hardware software separation where you're able to do multiple different kinds
of activity on the exact same machine. One of those are obviously computers that we use. The other is
our brains and nervous systems where we know the exact same architecture is able to learn lots of
different things and then to have behaviors that are strongly determined by their past history of
electrical experiences, basically. Right. So just to, just to make sure I've got it on the planarian
experiments you were describing. So the pattern memory is essentially distributed throughout the
organism. There's no like particular locus. Correct. And is that something that you knew when you, when you
started these experiments, or is that sort of part of the, part of the finding? We didn't, well, we
certainly didn't know it, but we expected it for two reasons. We expected it first because
planaria themselves have this kind of a very interesting holographic property where every,
pretty much every piece of the planaria knows what the whole planaria is supposed to look like.
So, so, so we already knew that an ideal solution to this problem is going to somehow show us why it
is that every piece knows what to do. And not every species of worm does this. There are species where
only the heads regenerate tails, but the tails can't make heads and so on. But the species that we work
on every region of the planaria knows what the whole thing looks like. So that, and also this idea
of distributed information in the brain, again, there's this amazing book called Shuffle Brain
by Paul Peach. And he talks about his attempts to find the locus of learned information in axolotls
by taking out various pieces of the brain and in fact, reshuffling them and so on, trying to find
out where it is. And he really found, in fact, the second half of his book is all about holography
because he basically was driven to that kind of model because the information seemed to be spread
everywhere. And that's, and that's a common theme that, you know, information is sort of
throughout neural networks. So the fact that this, this circuit was everywhere was, was expected.
The trick of course, is to show how it rescales, because if you have a planarian where the bioelectric
pattern goes head to tail, and now you've chopped off most of it, the remaining circuit has to rescale,
right? It has to reestablish that bioelectric pattern. And we now have some computational models
that show how that works. All right. Well, I'm going to resist the temptation to ask like 10
different thought experiments about what would happen if you did this or that to the planarian,
but okay. So this is a great setup for this whole suite of issues related to the idea of
scale-free cognition, basal cognition, cognition all the way down this, this area that you've been
really active in recently. So could you just, yeah, I mean, could you just set the stage for us
behind these ideas of scale-free cognition or cognition all the way down?
Yeah. One way to approach this issue, and certainly lots of people, big figures in philosophy
of mind and so on have weighed in on this question is to ask how do minds and bodies relate? So there
are certain, well, there's one body that you're sure of has a mind and that's your own. And there are
lots of other bodies that you're more or less, you're not certain, but you believe they also have
minds. And then there are all kinds of objects around you that may or may not, you know, some
of these are animals, they may be fish, they may be plants, they may be robots. They may be at
someday, they may be things that you encounter in outer space. They may be things you create in
synthetic biology. And we should talk about that a little bit, but, but, but there's a whole range
of objects around you. And one can ask this question of, are some of them cognitive the way that
we are meaning, do they have preferences or are they just following an algorithm? Do they have
memories? Do they have goals? All, all these kinds of things. And so there are lots of opinions about
how one should make that decision. And it's important because it also feeds into ethics,
right? Because the question of whether or not you think something is a machine, whatever that is,
we can, we can get into that versus something that is, that is cognitive in the same sense that
you and I are, you have different ethical obligations to it, right? So it's a big, it becomes
of practical concern. So the field of basal cognition asks us to take evolution seriously
and to say that, look, let's just start, we can start with humans and we can ask, okay,
we're pretty sure if anything is we are cognitive creatures. Let's track backwards. Where did that
come from? And so as you track backwards, you find a continuous, of course, you find a continuous
history going all the way back to the simplest forms of which are unicellular. And what you find is
that, at least I think, and that people have argued otherwise, but, but I think that there is
absolutely no privileged location where you could put a sharp line and say, okay, everything to the
right of this line is truly cognitive. Everything to the left of this line is at best as if, right?
It's, it may be acting in a smart way. It may be doing, you know, but, but, but there's no one
home. There's no cognition there. I think that's fundamentally mistaken. And so the view that,
that I and, and, and others have is that there's never any point in asking whether something is
cognitive, whether something has real memory, whether something has consciousness. The question
is how much, and we can get into the harder question of whether there's such a thing as zero.
And I'm not sure that there is, but that's a separate question. But the, the key, I think,
to all of this is that what gets us in trouble is, is a binary view of this. And almost any concept
that's related to this field is better handled as a continuum where you're not trying to divide
things into two binary categories, but you're asking how much and what kind. And then a lot
of things that are really pseudo problems go away. Okay. So let's, let's talk a little bit more
about this continuum. So we've got it anchored on the one end by humans. As you said, we will just
grant that we're obviously cognitive. So what do you see as the opposite end? What for you is kind of
the minimal form of cognition or the sort of simplest case of cognition that you would want to grant?
Yeah. So, so before I define what, what, that, that's a hard question that I'll, I'll, I'll tell
you what I think the minimum is, but, but before we get there, let's just look at the continuum a
little bit to just to get a, just to get a feel for what happens when you, when you shift down
towards that direction. I think that what's important to keep science moving forward and to
keep this field moving forward is to accept that we can't make armchair pronouncements about what
cognitive capacities things have. So not, not philosophy. We need a, we need a, an empirical
approach to this. And the way to do this, I think is a very akin to Dan Dennett's intentional stance,
